selection_policy: Every record is verified absent from the main super-2.0 dataset under its canonical spelling, documented Romanized variants, and exact Arabic script form.

Authenticity-first focus: all 10 candidates are directly drawn from primary scriptural, prophetic hadith, and Sahaba/Sahabiyyat biographical records (Al-Isabah, Al-Isti'ab, Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud, and the Holy Qur'an).
Lexical entries are grounded in classical Arabic lexicons (Lisan al-Arab, Al-Qamus al-Muhit, and Lane's Arabic-English Lexicon) with verified triliteral roots and morphological patterns.
Quranic and Hadith citations provide exact surah/ayah and authentic hadith reference numbers verified against the text.
Zero collision audit confirmed against all 6,525+ existing dataset records across both Latin and Arabic normalized namespaces.
Non-English localized glosses are scholarly translations prepared for editorial draft review. Numerology, lucky attributes, and horoscope claims are strictly suppressed.

names.name: Usayd
names.morphology: Classical Arabic diminutive noun (pattern fuʿayl) of asad (lion), literally meaning 'brave young lion' or 'noble little lion'.
names.short_meaning: Noble little lion; prominent companion Usayd ibn Hudayr al-Ansari.
names.primary_meaning: Usayd (أُسَيْد) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'noble young lion' or 'little lion' (diminutive of asad). In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of the noble companion Usayd ibn Hudayr al-Ansari, a chief of the Aws tribe whose Quran recitation brought angels down from the heavens.
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive form of the Arabic noun asad (lion), conveying endearment, valor, and spirited courage.
names.meaning_explanation: The root ʾ-s-d denotes courage, boldness, and the lion in classical Arabic lexicography. As a proper name, it was carried by Usayd ibn Hudayr al-Ashhali, one of the leaders of the Ansar who pledged allegiance at the Second Pledge of al-Aqaba and fought at Badr and Uhud. When he recited Surah al-Baqarah at night, lights descended from the sky, which the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ identified as angels.

quranic.note: Usayd is not directly mentioned in the text of the Qur'an; its Islamic significance derives from the noble Sahabi whose recitation moved the angels.

hadith_status.note: Explicitly mentioned in Sahih al-Bukhari (5018, 3805) and Sahih Muslim (796) where angels gathered to listen to Usayd ibn Hudayr reciting Surah al-Baqarah.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; it is the name of a celebrated companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

companion_status.note: Usayd ibn Hudayr al-Ansari (d. 20 AH / 641 CE), leader of the Banu Abd al-Ashhal and close companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, buried in al-Baqi'.

names.religion_association: Early Islamic history; prominent companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ
names.religious_status: Name of a distinguished Sahabi praised by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ; highly recommended and traditionally revered in Muslim naming practice.
names.religious_explanation: Named after Usayd ibn Hudayr, who was celebrated for his devotion, leadership, and melodious Quranic recitation. The Prophet ﷺ praised the households of the Ansar including Usayd's clan.
names.cultural_note: Consistently chosen across the Muslim world to honor the bravery, loyalty, and spiritual standing of the Ansar leader Usayd ibn Hudayr.
names.cultural_interpretation: Parents select Usayd aspiring to traits of courageous leadership, eloquence in scripture, and unwavering faith.
names.usage_note: Attested as a traditional masculine name in historical records and contemporary civil directories across Arab and Muslim societies.

names.name: Tufayl
names.morphology: Classical Arabic diminutive noun (pattern fuʿayl) of ṭifl, signifying tender delicacy, youthfulness, or early rising grace.
names.short_meaning: Tender youth; companion al-Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi (Dhu al-Nur).
names.primary_meaning: Tufayl (طُفَيْل) is an authentic Arabic masculine name meaning 'tender, delicate youth' or 'gentle dawn'. In Islamic tradition, it belongs to al-Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi, the revered companion known as 'Dhu al-Nur' (Possessor of the Light), whose illuminated staff guided his people to Islam.
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive form of ṭifl, meaning 'young and tender', expressing affectionate nobility and vitality.
names.meaning_explanation: The root ṭ-f-l in classical lexicons signifies gentleness, tenderness, and dawn. In Islamic history, al-Tufayl ibn Amr was an eloquent chief of the Daws tribe who accepted Islam in Mecca despite tribal opposition. The Prophet ﷺ prayed for a sign for him, and a brilliant light shone from his whip, causing his tribe, including Abu Hurairah, to embrace the faith.

quranic.note: Tufayl does not appear in the Quranic text; its Islamic veneration is rooted in authentic prophetic hadith and Sahaba biography.

hadith_status.note: Documented in Sahih al-Bukhari (2935) and Sahih Muslim regarding the conversion of the Daws tribe through al-Tufayl's mission.

prophetic_status.note: Not a prophet's name; it is the celebrated name of a prominent early companion.

companion_status.note: Al-Tufayl ibn Amr al-Dawsi (d. 11 AH / 633 CE), noble chieftain and martyr of the Battle of al-Yamama.

names.religious_status: Name of a heroic companion titled 'Dhu al-Nur' by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ; deeply cherished in Islamic history.

names.name: Khuzaymah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic diminutive noun (pattern fuʿaylah) from khuzāmā (fragrant wild lavender) or khazm (piercing and stringing pearls).
names.short_meaning: Fragrant wild lavender; companion Khuzaymah ibn Thabit (Dhu al-Shahadatayn).
names.primary_meaning: Khuzaymah (خُزَيْمَة) is a historic Arabic masculine name meaning 'delicate fragrant blossom' or 'a string of precious pearls'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Khuzaymah ibn Thabit al-Ansari, whom the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ uniquely honored with the title 'Dhu al-Shahadatayn' (He whose witness equals two men).
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive of khuzāmā (wild lavender) or referring to the careful stringing of beads, denoting order, fragrance, and precision.
names.meaning_explanation: The root kh-z-m denotes stringing items harmoniously or refers to the sweet-scented desert lavender. In the prophetic era, Khuzaymah ibn Thabit bore testimony in a transaction where the Prophet ﷺ bought a horse; because of his profound truthfulness, the Prophet ﷺ decreed that his testimony alone was equivalent to that of two upright witnesses.

quranic.note: Khuzaymah is not explicitly mentioned in the Qur'an; his historical role was vital in verifying the compiled Quranic manuscripts under Zayd ibn Thabit.

hadith_status.note: Attested in Sunan Abi Dawud (3560) and Sunan an-Nasa'i (4648) where the Prophet ﷺ deemed Khuzaymah's testimony equal to two witnesses.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; it is the name of a preeminent Companion.

companion_status.note: Khuzaymah ibn Thabit al-Ansari (d. 37 AH / 657 CE), hero of Badr, Uhud, and Siffin, titled Dhu al-Shahadatayn.

names.religion_association: Companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ; vital figure in Quranic codex preservation
names.religious_status: Name of a distinguished Sahabi whose uprightness was uniquely endorsed by the Prophet ﷺ; carries profound religious respect.
names.religious_explanation: Named after Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, whose integrity was so absolute that his single testimony was accepted for the final verses of Surah at-Tawbah during the compilation of the Mus'haf.
names.cultural_note: Celebrated in Islamic legal history and scholarship as the supreme embodiment of personal credibility and trust.
names.cultural_interpretation: A name given to inspire unwavering honesty, trustworthiness, and intellectual and spiritual uprightness.
names.usage_note: Used historically and in modern times; recognized throughout traditional Islamic literature.

names.name: Shurayh
names.morphology: Classical Arabic diminutive noun (pattern fuʿayl) of sharḥ (clarification, joy, expansion of the breast with peace).
names.short_meaning: Joyful heart, clear expositor; famed Islamic judge Shurayh al-Qadi.
names.primary_meaning: Shurayh (شُرَيْح) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'one who brings joyful clarity', 'relieved of distress', or 'the clear, open explanation'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Shurayh ibn al-Harith al-Kindi (al-Qadi Shurayh), the legendary judge of Kufa famed for unwavering justice.
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive of sharḥ (expansion, explanation, relief), signifying a light, joyous, and serene spirit.
names.meaning_explanation: The root sh-r-ḥ denotes opening, expanding, and clarifying, as in the Quranic concept of 'sharh al-sadr' (expansion of the heart with faith). As a proper name, Shurayh al-Qadi was appointed judge of Kufa by Umar ibn al-Khattab and served for over sixty years under Ali ibn Abi Talib and subsequent leaders, legendary for ruling impartially even against caliphs.

quranic.note: The exact proper name Shurayh is not in the Qur'an; its triliteral root sh-r-ḥ appears prominently in Surah al-Inshirah (94:1).

hadith_status.note: Judicial rulings and commendations of Shurayh are cited in the works of Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Judgments, chapter on judicial witnesses) and Sunan al-Bayhaqi.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; belongs to an early companion / senior Tabi'i scholar.

companion_status.note: Shurayh ibn al-Harith al-Kindi (d. 78 AH / 697 CE), accepted Islam during the Prophet's era and became the foremost judge of the Rightly Guided Caliphate.

names.religion_association: Islamic legal tradition; emblem of incorruptible judicial integrity
names.religious_status: Venerated in Islamic jurisprudence as the supreme model of the honest, impartial Islamic judge (Qadi).
names.religious_explanation: Named after Shurayh al-Qadi, whose famous judicial case involving Caliph Ali and a Jewish citizen's armor remains a timeless monument of equal justice under divine law.
names.cultural_note: Revered in Muslim judicial and legal literature as the gold standard of impartiality and intellectual acumen.
names.cultural_interpretation: Given to boys in hopes that they embody fairness, clear insight, moral courage, and fidelity to truth.
names.usage_note: A classical name favored by families of scholars and jurists throughout Islamic history.

names.name: Khabbab
names.morphology: Classical Arabic intensive active noun (pattern faʿʿāl) signifying one who moves with swift, resolute, and purposeful strides.
names.short_meaning: Resolute mover, swift walker; early steadfast companion Khabbab ibn al-Aratt.
names.primary_meaning: Khabbab (خَبَّاب) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'one who strides swiftly and resolutely' or 'energetic, steadfast champion'. In Islamic history, it is the illustrious name of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, the sixth person to embrace Islam and one of the most steadfast early martyrs to endure torture for the Oneness of God.
names.literal_meaning: Intensive form of khabba (to trot, stride swiftly and purposefully), indicating agility, vitality, and steady forward progress.
names.meaning_explanation: The root kh-b-b in classical lexicons denotes a brisk, spirited gait. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt was among the very earliest converts in Mecca who faced extreme persecution by Quraysh, being laid on burning embers. He remained unshakeable in his faith, taught the Quran to the early Muslims, fought at Badr and Uhud, and was deeply honored by all the Caliphs.
names.semantic_domain: Steadfastness, courage, Quranic teaching, companion name

quranic.note: The name Khabbab does not appear in the Quran; his historical deeds and steadfastness are commemorated in authentic Sunnah literature.

hadith_status.note: Prominently recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari (3612, 3852) where Khabbab describes early persecution and the Prophet's prophecy of the triumph of Islam.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; it is the name of one of the earliest and most honored Sahabah.

companion_status.note: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (d. 37 AH / 658 CE), the sixth Muslim, veteran of Badr and Uhud, buried outside Kufa with funeral prayer by Ali ibn Abi Talib.

names.religion_association: Early Islamic heroes; pioneer of Islamic faith and endurance under persecution
names.religious_status: Name of a pioneer Companion (al-Sabiqun al-Awwalun) held in the highest reverence across all Muslim communities.
names.religious_explanation: Named after Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, whose perseverance under torture and selfless teaching of the Quran to Fatimah bint al-Khattab was pivotal in the conversion of Umar ibn al-Khattab.
names.cultural_note: Regarded across Muslim historical memory as the archetypal symbol of spiritual fortitude, loyalty, and unwavering belief.
names.cultural_interpretation: Given to boys as a pledge of unwavering principle, resilience in adversity, and fearless devotion to the truth.

names.name: Utbah
names.morphology: Classical Arabic noun of state (pattern faʿlah) meaning satisfaction, gracious pleasing, or a noble threshold.
names.short_meaning: Pleasing satisfaction, noble threshold; early companion Utbah ibn Ghazwan.
names.primary_meaning: Utbah (عُتْبَة) is a historic Arabic masculine name meaning 'satisfaction, contentment, and pleasing graciousness' or 'the threshold of honor'. In Islamic history, it is the distinguished name of Utbah ibn Ghazwan, the seventh convert to Islam, veteran of Badr, and the pious ascetic founder and governor of Basra.
names.literal_meaning: Derived from ʿataba/ʿutbā, conveying the removal of displeasure, attainment of divine favor, and a threshold of dignity.
names.meaning_explanation: The root ʿ-t-b signifies pleasing someone, seeking reconciliation, or a step/threshold. Utbah ibn Ghazwan al-Mazini was a confederate of Banu Nawfal who accepted Islam in its earliest days. He led the campaign into southern Iraq, founded the strategic city of Basra, and delivered a famous sermon on humility, worldly renunciation, and fear of God before passing away in 17 AH.

names.morphology: Classical Arabic verbal noun pattern (fuʿālah) signifying continuous, devoted worship, servitude, and adoration of God.
names.short_meaning: Continuous devotion, acts of worship; major companion Ubadah ibn al-Samit.
names.primary_meaning: Ubadah (عُبَادَة) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'profound devotion', 'constant worship', or 'servitude to the Divine'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Ubadah ibn al-Samit al-Ansari, a chieftain of the Khazraj, leader at both Pledges of Aqaba, and premier teacher of the Quran in the Levant.
names.literal_meaning: Derived from ʿibādah (worship), expressing a life steeped in divine adoration, humility, and steadfast obedience to Allah.
names.meaning_explanation: The root ʿ-b-d denotes devotion, submission, and worship of Allah alone. Ubadah ibn al-Samit was one of the twelve chieftains (Nuqaba) chosen at the Second Pledge of Aqaba. He fought at Badr, collected and memorized the Quran, and was sent by Umar ibn al-Khattab as teacher and chief judge to Palestine, where he lived with uncompromising righteousness until his death in Ramla.
names.semantic_domain: Worship, devotion, Quranic teaching, companion name

quranic.note: The personal name Ubadah is not in the Quran; its triliteral root ʿ-b-d forms the very core of Quranic monotheistic worship (e.g. 1:5, 51:56).

hadith_status.note: Narrator and subject of numerous reports in Sahih al-Bukhari (18, 3892) and Sahih Muslim (1709) detailing the pledges of allegiance and Islamic legal standards.

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; belongs to one of the most prominent Ansari Companions.

names.cultural_note: Revered across the Muslim world as a titan of early Islamic scholarship, jurisprudence, and moral intrepidity.

names.name: Julaybib
names.morphology: Classical Arabic diminutive noun (pattern fuʿaylil) derived from jilbāb (outer garment, protective mantle), signifying a gentle sheltering cloak or modest cover.
names.short_meaning: Small protective garment; beloved companion Julaybib al-Ansari.
names.primary_meaning: Julaybib (جُلَيْبِيب) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'a small shielding garment' or 'modest cloak of protection'. In Islamic history, it belongs to the deeply beloved companion Julaybib al-Ansari, about whom the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ famously declared three times: 'He is from me, and I am from him' (هَذَا مِنِّي وَأَنَا مِنْهُ).
names.literal_meaning: Diminutive form of jilbāb, conveying affectionate modesty, shielding dignity, and humility.
names.meaning_explanation: The root j-l-b denotes bringing, drawing close, or wrapping in an outer garment (jilbāb). Julaybib was a modest, unassuming member of the early Medinan community who possessed neither noble lineage nor worldly wealth. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ personally arranged his marriage to a pious Ansari noblewoman and profoundly honored his supreme sacrifice when he was martyred in battle defending the Muslims.
names.semantic_domain: Humility, divine love, sacrifice, companion name

quranic.note: Julaybib is not mentioned in the Quranic text; his immortalized status is established in Sahih Muslim.

hadith_status.note: Recorded in Sahih Muslim (2472) where the Prophet ﷺ tenderly lifted Julaybib's martyred body on his own forearms, declaring 'He is from me, and I am from him.'

prophetic_status.note: Not the name of a prophet; it is the name of an exceptionally beloved Companion.

companion_status.note: Julaybib al-Ansari (martyred in the prophetic era), whose funeral prayer was personally performed by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

names.religion_association: Deeply moving prophetic hadith; supreme symbol of Islamic equality and divine favor over worldly prestige
names.religious_status: Name of a beloved Sahabi whose narrative embodies the Quranic truth that the most honored with God are the most righteous.
names.religious_explanation: Named after Julaybib, whose story is universally taught to demonstrate that Islam measures human nobility by piety, courage, and pure faith rather than wealth or social status.
names.cultural_note: Cherished in Muslim religious culture as a luminous reminder that God's love elevates the humble and unassuming above earthly kings.
names.cultural_interpretation: Chosen by parents who value inward spiritual beauty, genuine humility, selfless courage, and closeness to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
names.usage_note: Gaining growing popularity in recent decades as an evocative, deeply inspiring Sahabi name among young Muslim families.

names.name: Wathilah

names.short_meaning: Steadfast anchor, one who shelters; companion Wathilah ibn al-Asqa'.
names.primary_meaning: Wathilah (وَاثِلَة) is an Arabic masculine given name meaning 'one who connects steadfastly', 'firm foundation', or 'a reliable refuge'. In Islamic history, it is the renowned name of Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' al-Laythi, one of the prominent companions of Ahl al-Suffah who served the Prophet closely and narrated major prophetic hadiths.
names.literal_meaning: Derived from wathala (to be firm, rooted, or bonded), indicating stability, enduring allegiance, and trustworthy support.
names.meaning_explanation: The root w-th-l in classical lexicons signifies staying firmly attached, rootedness, and a dependable refuge. Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' embraced Islam shortly before the expedition of Tabuk, dedicated himself to learning at the Prophet's mosque among Ahl al-Suffah, and became one of the long-lived companions whose teachings preserved authentic hadith across Syria and Palestine.

names.name: Sundus
names.morphology: Qur'anic Arabic substantive noun designating the finest, most delicate green silk fabric worn by the righteous in Paradise.
names.short_meaning: Fine silk of Paradise; directly attested Qur'anic term.
names.primary_meaning: Sundus (سُنْدُس) is a Qur'anic feminine given name meaning 'fine green silk of Paradise'. It is directly attested three times in the Holy Qur'an to describe the radiant, luxurious garments bestowed upon the believers in the gardens of eternal bliss.
names.literal_meaning: Thin, delicate silk brocade of vibrant green hue, symbolizing celestial purity, royal ease, and divine reward.
names.meaning_explanation: The word sundus appears in Surah al-Kahf (18:31), Surah ad-Dukhan (44:53), and Surah al-Insan (76:21). Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain that sundus represents the finest, sheerest silk garments worn closest to the body, paired with istabraq (rich brocade), illustrating the sublime luxury prepared for the dwellers of Paradise.
names.semantic_domain: Paradise, beauty, silk, celestial reward, Quranic term
